title: Probiotic Trial Reader
description: Interactive simulation of probiotic clinical trials. A made-up probiotic has a small true effect; each simulated trial adds random chance and reports its best-looking outcome as one dot on an effect-size axis. Learners change people per group, the number of outcomes measured, and whether there is a placebo group, and see how small trials, many outcomes, and missing controls produce impressive-looking but inflated results.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: neuroscience (gut-brain axis)
publisher: Gut Check: The Neuroscience of How Your Gut and Brain Talk
learningObjectives: Judge how trial size changes how close a reported effect is likely to be to the true effect.
Explain why measuring many outcomes and reporting the best one inflates results, and why trials name a primary outcome in advance.
Explain why a placebo group is needed to separate a treatment's effect from the placebo response.
keyQuestions: Why can a small trial report a big effect for a treatment that does very little?
What happens to reported results when a trial measures many outcomes and reports the best one?
What does a placebo group protect against?
Which trial designs deserve the most confidence?
misconceptions: A single study that found a significant result proves the treatment works.
A bigger reported effect from a small study is more convincing than a smaller effect from a large study.
If people improved after taking a probiotic, the probiotic caused the improvement.
Measuring more outcomes makes a study more thorough and therefore more trustworthy.
